data.caption: Feel like yourself again
data.copy:
My mother never drank.

She had one glass of wine a year at Christmas. She died at 63 of the disease everyone told her only alcoholics got. Her doctor called it "mild" for twelve years — because he was watching her ALT, which never went above 68, while her liver was quietly scarring itself into cirrhosis. If your fatty liver has been "mild" for the last three years, please read this before he says it one more time.

I want to tell you the day I found out.

I went to close out my mother's medical file six weeks after her funeral. Her doctor's office had left a message about paperwork. I drove over on a Tuesday morning. And while I sat in the exam room waiting for the receptionist to bring the file, I read through the last ten years of my mother's charts.

Her ALT at age 51: 41. "Stable." Her ALT at age 55: 47. "Stable." Her ALT at age 58: 52. "Stable." Her ALT at age 60: 61. "Stable." Her ALT at age 62: 68. "Slightly elevated. Monitor."

Twelve years of "stable." Twelve years of "come back in a year." Twelve years of the same paragraph copy-pasted at the bottom of every visit summary: "Fatty liver — mild. Recommend weight management. Follow up as needed."

She died at 63 in a hospital bed from sudden ascites — her belly filled with fluid over six weeks. Her doctor called it "acute decompensation." What that meant in plain English was that her liver had been scarring itself into cirrhosis while everyone was watching a number that would never move until it was already too late.

I sat in that exam room for a long time. And then I went home, and I opened the drawer where I keep my own lab reports.

Mine was 41. And "stable."

I am 47.

I had not zipped up a pair of jeans in fifteen months. I lived in stretchy skirts and long cardigans. My husband had stopped putting his hand on my waist when we walked — because there was nowhere flat left for his hand to rest. My daughter had asked me at Thanksgiving if I was pregnant. I said no. She did not ask me anything else…

data.caption: jevawell.com
data.copy:
My wife quit her GLP-1 medication eleven months ago after one bad month.

She has had explosive diarrhea every week since.

We thought stopping would fix it. Stopping made nothing change.

I am writing this because last weekend my wife sat in a gas-station bathroom for thirty-five minutes while I waited in the car in the parking lot of a Shell station.

We were twenty-two minutes from a baby shower for her niece.

She had picked out the dress three weeks ago.

She came back to the car and said, "Just take me home."

She did not cry on the way home.

She cried that night.

She said, "It has been a year. I am done waiting for this to fix itself."

That is the night I stopped trusting what every doctor had told us for the last twelve months.

Anika is fifty-one.

We have been married twenty-seven years.

She was a normal weight her whole twenties. After our second was born she could never get the last forty pounds off, no matter what she tried.

Around the start of last year her primary care put her on a GLP-1.

The titration went 0.25 milligrams. Then 0.5. Then 1.0. Then 1.7.

The first three doses were fine.

Mild nausea. Mild constipation she fixed with Miralax and moved on.

She lost thirty-eight pounds in about nine months.

She was happy.

She was fitting back into jeans she had not worn since our second kid was born.

She was dancing in the kitchen again.

Then they moved her up to the 1.7.

By day four of that dose she had loose stools.

By the end of the second week she was running to the bathroom three or four times a day.

The third week she had to abandon her grocery cart in the middle of the produce section.

She quit the medication in week four.

I supported it.

We both thought she would be back to normal by Memorial Day.

Memorial Day came.

The diarrhea did not stop.

Fourth of July came.

It did not stop.

Our anniversary in October came.

It changed shape. It went from daily to weekly.

But weekly meant she could not plan a single thing.

Because she…

data.caption: Read this if you have kids or grandkids
data.copy:
I coach a nationally ranked academic quiz team. My 12-year-olds can name every planet's moons, every human bone, every capital on Earth. Last month at practice, I turned off the buzzers and asked one question that wasn't in any packet: What's something nobody knows yet that you wish somebody would figure out? Eight kids. Over 300 trophies between them. Ninety seconds of silence. Then my best player raised his hand and asked, "Will this be at regionals?"

I've coached this team for 11 years, and I need to confess something about my own sport.

Parents drive 2 hours each way for our practices. They pay tournament fees, hotel weekends, private study packets. They do it because a quiz kid looks like the dream. A child who knows everything. A walking encyclopedia at the dinner table. Proof, in trophy form, that the curiosity is thriving.

I believed that too, for about 9 of my 11 years.

Here's what finally broke it for me. In quiz bowl, the whole skill is buzzing in before the question finishes. My kids train on it for hours. The moderator starts, "This celestial body, whose surface features include..." and BZZT, a 12-year-old says "Europa," and he's right, and the room applauds.

Watch that moment the way I finally watched it last season.

The question never gets to exist. My kids are so fast that no question is ever fully asked in their presence. I have spent 11 years, thousands of hours, training children to kill questions before the question mark arrives. That is the actual sport. Interrupting questions with answers.

And it works. We win. We beat schools 3 times our size.

Last month I ran the experiment I'd been avoiding. No buzzers night. I told them: tonight, no answers allowed. Only questions. Ask me anything you've ever wondered. Ask something nobody knows. First kid to stump the coach picks the pizza.

These are the 8 most knowledgeable children in the state, in their age group. That is not an exaggeration, there's a ranking, I can show you.

data.caption: Read this if you have kids or grandkids
data.copy:
I run school field trips at a science museum that families pay $30 a ticket to visit. Last Tuesday, I stood 60 kids in front of a real 65-million-year-old dinosaur skeleton and asked one question: What do you want to know about it? Sixty kids. Four stories of bone. Not one question. They took photos of it and asked when lunch was.

I've worked in museum education for 11 years.

Schools bus kids to us from 3 states. Parents chaperone on their day off. Everyone believes the same thing, that if you put a child in front of something amazing, wonder just happens.

Last Tuesday, I tried something I'd never attempted. Instead of my usual tour script, I ran what I privately called the One Question Game. At each stop, no facts from me, just: what do you want to know about this?

The dinosaur hall. The real moon rock. The tornado machine.

I watched 60 fourth and fifth graders stand in silence.

At the moon rock, one boy finally raised his hand. "Is it real?" I said yes, brought back by astronauts. He said "cool" and looked back at his phone case, which he'd been decorating with stickers.

At the tornado machine, a girl asked if we sold slime in the gift shop.

Sixty kids. Three of the most extraordinary objects a child can stand in front of. The whole game produced 2 questions, and one of them was about slime.

These weren't struggling kids. Their teacher told me proudly on the way in that this was the advanced group. Reading above grade level. Great test scores.

I ate my lunch in the staff room staring at my tour clipboard and felt sick. Their school spent $1,800 busing them to us. The parents paid $30 a head. Everyone believes proximity to amazing things builds curious kids.

It doesn't.

We're running a generation of children past the most incredible objects on Earth, and they've lost the muscle you need to care. They can photograph anything. They can't wonder about it.

That evening, I couldn't get the silent dinosaur hall out of my head.

My son Eli is 9. He's grown up…

data.caption: Limited Time Offer
data.copy:
I've handled over 600 divorces in 18 years of practicing family law.

I can tell you the exact moment a woman decides to leave. The look in her eyes changes. Something switches off and doesn't switch back on. I've seen it so many times I can spot it before she says a word.

But that's not what I want to talk about.

I want to talk about what happens to her face in the six months after.

Nobody talks about this. Not therapists. Not doctors. Not the women themselves.

I'm going to. Because I've watched it happen to over 600 women and I'm done pretending it's not a pattern.

I noticed it about eight years into my practice.

I started seeing a woman — let's call her Client A — in January. She was 52. She came into my office looking like a normal, put-together, 52-year-old woman. Good skin. Dressed nicely. Alert. Present.

We met every two weeks to work through the divorce proceedings. Her husband had left for a coworker. Standard devastation. Nothing I hadn't seen before.

By March, something was different.

It wasn't her weight, though she'd lost some. It wasn't her clothes, though those had gotten looser.

It was her skin.

In two months, her skin had changed so drastically that if you showed me her January photo and her March photo, I'd have told you they were five years apart.

The color was gone. Gray. Dull. Like the life had drained out of her face.

Lines had appeared that weren't there in January. Not smile lines. Stress fractures. Deep grooves between her eyebrows. Creases around her mouth that aged her a decade.

Her eyes were sunken. Not from crying, though she was doing plenty of that. From somewhere deeper. Like her face was collapsing inward.

I'd seen it before. I just hadn't named it.

After Client A, I started paying attention. And once I saw the pattern, I couldn't unsee it.

I call it Divorce Face.

I don't use that term in my office. I'd never say it to a client. But in my own notes, that's what I call it.

It's not metaphorical. It's not emotion…

data.caption: Feel Like Yourself Again
data.copy:
I'm so f***ing sick of my doctor handing me a Lisinopril prescription like she's doing me a favor.

Every single visit.

I sit down. Three minutes of small talk. She puts the cuff on my arm. Sighs at the number. And before I've even buttoned my shirt back up, she's scribbling the same prescription she's probably written six hundred times this year.

Lisinopril.

Like it's the answer to a question she didn't bother to ask.

Like the only thing that could possibly be wrong with me is the one thing her pad can fix.

She did it to me three weeks ago. 148 over 92. She didn't ask me what I'd already tried. Didn't ask what my mother had been on. Didn't ask anything. She just reached for the pad and started writing.

And the only thing I could see while she was writing was my mother.

My mother spent twelve years on Lisinopril. Twelve years.

She was sixty-one when she started it. She moved like she was eighty by the time she was sixty-four.

The dry cough first. That awful hacking cough that hit her at three in the morning and didn't stop until the sun came up. The kind of cough where she'd hold her ribs because it hurt to breathe.

Then the dizziness. She fell twice. Once in the kitchen, once on the bathroom tile. The second one split her eyebrow open and I drove her to the ER at midnight while she held a dish towel to her face.

Then the swelling. Her ankles puffed up so badly she couldn't wear her real shoes anymore. She wore slippers to my daughter's wedding. She was furious about it. She'd been waiting two years for that day.

And then the part nobody talks about. The fog. My mother used to do the Sunday crossword in pen. By year four on that medication she couldn't remember the word for refrigerator. She'd point at it and say "the cold thing."

And by the end she couldn't do anything on her own.

My father drove her everywhere because the dizziness made it dangerous for her to get behind the wheel.

data.caption: His psychiatrist prescribed Concerta in 6th grade. Nobody told me about the sleep tax.
data.copy:
I have been feeding my 13-year-old prescription amphetamines every morning for three years.

He has the grades.

He does not sleep anymore.

Nobody warned me what was being traded for what.

-----

I'm not against ADHD medication.

Let me say that first.

Concerta saved my son's grades.

It saved his self-esteem.

It saved his teacher's sanity.

He went from D's to B's in one semester.

He stopped getting in trouble in class.

He stopped crying about homework.

I am grateful for Concerta every single day.

-----

But here is what no one tells you when you start.

Not the pediatrician.

Not the psychiatrist.

Not the pharmacist.

Not the school nurse.

Not the prescription insert.

ADHD stimulants are paid for at night.

His brain pays the tax.

And nobody warned me.

-----

By the second year on Concerta he stopped falling asleep before 1am.

The psychiatrist shrugged.

She said "give him melatonin."

The pediatrician shrugged.

She said "give him melatonin."

The pharmacist said "is one or three milligrams better."

She didn't ask me why I was buying it for a teenager.

She didn't ask me how long.

She didn't ask me anything.

-----

We tried 1mg.

Worked for 4 days.

3mg.

Worked for 6 days.

5mg.

Worked for one week then he was groggy until 2pm on a Saturday.

I switched brands.

Three different brands.

I bought one off Amazon, one from Target, one from a "premium" brand my friend swore by.

Each one worked for a few days and stopped.

Each time he needed more.

Each time the morning got worse.

-----

By year three on Concerta my son could not fall asleep without 10mg of melatonin.

Twice the adult dose.

And it still wasn't really working.

He was just unconscious.

He'd wake up at 5am with the cortisol panic.

Then crash at 10am.

He'd be a zombie until lunch.

The Concerta would kick in at 11.

He'd hyperfocus all afternoon.

Then we'd start the whole thing over again at 11pm.

I was watching my child get sicker on the protocol the medical system gave him.
…

data.caption: Support stamina and heart health every day
data.copy:
I Stopped Picking Up My Grandson Eighteen Months Ago. He's Four. He's Started Asking Why.

I'm 58.

I have a daughter, a son-in-law, and one grandson. His name is Theo. He'll be five in November.

Up until about eighteen months ago I picked him up every single time I saw him. It wasn't a thing. It was just what you do.

Then it was a thing.

Then I stopped doing it.

He hasn't asked his mother. He's asked me directly. Twice now.

The first time was in October. He held his arms up at the front door when I came over for Sunday dinner and I knelt down to hug him instead and he said: "Grandpa. Why don't you pick me up anymore?"

I told him grandpa's back was tired.

He said: "Oh. Okay."

He went and got his trucks out of the bin.

The second time was three weeks ago, in his backyard. He'd climbed up on the picnic table and asked me to lift him down. I lifted him with one hand under each armpit and set him on the grass, and the second the weight came off my back I made a noise without meaning to. Not a word. A sound.

He looked up at me from the grass and he said: "Did that hurt?"

I told him no.

He said: "Are you fibbing?"

He'd just learned the word "fibbing" that week.

I told him yes. I was fibbing. It hurt a little.

He thought about it for a second. Then he said, in the serious way four-year-olds say things they're trying out for the first time: "Maybe you should not pick me up if it hurts your back."

I said okay.

He patted my hand. The way his mother does.

He went off to play.

I stood there in my daughter's backyard and I had a moment I'm going to write down.

I had it because I'd just been parented by a four-year-old.

He'd been gentler about it than I'd been gentle with myself in two years.

I'm going to back up.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
